video_title: Terence Tao on Proof, Beauty, and the Future of Mathematics
transcript: TYLER COWEN: Hello, everyone, and welcome  back to Conversations with Tyler. Today,   I’m very happy to be speaking with Terry  Tao. He has a new and excellent book out,   Six Math Essentials. Terry is arguably the  greatest mathematician of his generation.   He is a Fields Medal winner, a professor  of mathematics at UCLA, and he has done   research in topics as varied as harmonic  analysis, partial differential equations,   algebraic combinatorics, arithmetic combinatorics,  geometric combinatorics, probability theory,   compressed sensing, analytic number theory, and  he writes a blog, and much more. Terry, welcome. TERENCE TAO: Oh, pleasure to be here. COWEN: Now, people often think  of mathematics as about logic,   but I’d like to start by asking you about  emotions. I’ll name a few results in math,   and you tell me what emotions  they evoke in you, okay? TAO: All right. COWEN: Euler’s identity. TAO: That is a very pretty and neat identity.  It connects all the fundamental constants of   mathematics: e, π, i, and 1 and 0. Actually,  to me, what is most beautiful about it is that   what it’s really saying is that rotation  is actually a type of multiplication.   Euler’s formula, you can think of it as eiπ  = −1. This is one form of Euler’s formula. When you exponentiate, raise e to something,  it’s like you’re multiplying something over   and over again. Compound interest is one  place where exponentiation shows up. The i   shifts things from just multiplying to  make things bigger or smaller, but instead,   we’re multiplying at right angles and making  it rotating. eiπ is saying that if you rotate   something by π, π radians, you flip it. It  becomes the negative of what you start with.   It actually connects geometry and dynamics  and algebra. It’s a very beautiful formula. COWEN: When you ponder quantum  mechanics, what do you feel? TAO: Oh, yes. COWEN: For me, it’s puzzlement,  but you’re smarter than I am. TAO: It uses very abstract mathematics,  the mathematics of Hilbert spaces,   which are these infinite-dimensional vector  spaces, and complex numbers. You definitely   need a fair bit of mathematical training to  understand the mathematics. It also forces you to   really change your idea of what reality is.  It’s like how we used to think that the Earth   was stationary, and then we had to change  our perspective and think of the Earth as   moving. Before quantum mechanics, we  used to think of physical objects as   always only being in one state. A light  is on or off. The cat is alive or dead. In order for the equations of quantum mechanics  to work, you have to accept that, in fact,   most of the time, objects live in superpositions.  A cat is neither alive nor dead, but a mixture of   both. They interact with each other in funny  ways, like how waves can interfere with each   other. It is a very unintuitive way  of thinking about reality because we   don’t see ourselves in superpositions, but the  math actually works out. Despite everything,   it actually is a better way  of explaining the world,   especially at a molecular level. It is very  mysterious, and it was very controversial when   it first came out. A lot of physicists did  not accept what the math was telling them. COWEN: The Riemann hypothesis, what do you feel? TAO: Oh, yes. That is a really big prize in  mathematics. Actually, recently we’re getting   some progress on that. That’s another story.  It concerns one of the most basic objects in   mathematics, the prime numbers, which we  now use prime numbers all over the place,   like in cryptography. For instance, a lot of  cryptographic protocols that we use to encrypt   our finances and whatever rely on properties of  the prime numbers. We look at the prime numbers,   and they behave very randomly. Sometimes they’re  close together, sometimes they’re far apart. The Riemann hypothesis is a very precise way  of quantifying this random-looking nature of   the primes, and it has many, many consequences.  Any part of mathematics that touches the primes,   if you know the Riemann hypothesis,  normally your results get stronger.   There’s a large chunk of results in number  theory which are conditional. If you have   the Riemann hypothesis, you get this good  result. Otherwise, we can’t say anything. Out of all the results, open questions in  mathematics, most open questions in mathematics,   they’re like puzzles. We don’t solve them for  their own sake. They’re useful for gaining   insight and help us eventually understand more  realistic, real-world problems. The Riemann   hypothesis is one of the few mathematical  questions which is actually quite useful   for its own sake. Knowing that it’s true  would actually imply a lot of other things. COWEN: You think it will be proven, can be proven? TAO: We are making progress.  In fact, just two days ago,   there was a significant advance on the Riemann  hypothesis. We are still quite a ways from the   full resolution, but now there are new ideas.  Unfortunately, the ideas were generated by AI,   and we don’t yet understand them. This is  part of the new era now. We are getting   answers without understanding, which  is a very strange era to be in. Historically, the only way to make a progress  on a difficult mathematical problem was to   understand it, and you could communicate these  insights to others. Now we have these machines   that can give us answers, but we have to  really work much harder than normal to   extract out the useful insights from them. It  is a strange era. We now have these new tools,   and hopefully we will have lots of mathematicians  exploring both old methods and new methods,   and we will find something. It  will probably require a new idea   which we haven’t seen before. We know the  limits of many of the existing techniques. COWEN: Gödel’s incompleteness  theorem, does it frustrate you? TAO: Yes. Mathematics is going through a crisis  right now. There was a similar crisis 100 years   ago. David Hilbert, who was one of the leading  mathematicians in the early 20th century,   had this great dream finding that every  single open problem in mathematics should   be solved or unsolved. We should systematically  try to answer all the questions in our subject.   Here’s a famous quote in German: “Wir müssen  wissen, und wir werden wissen,” “we must know,   and we will know.” Now, this was the  rallying cry for mathematics in 1900. Gödel proved this very, very striking result  that no matter how you set out the rules of   mathematics, there will always be statements  that cannot be proven or disproven from those   rules alone. That there is no fixed set of laws  of logic that can answer every single question.   They will always be incomplete. This was very  traumatic for mathematicians. It said that   Hilbert’s program would never be finished in some  sense. Over time, I think, we acclimatized to it. In practice, many of the results that we  do care about, we can prove or disprove.   The specific statements that Gödel showed  which were not provable or decidable are   not the ones that we encounter in real  life. Sometimes there are questions that   you can’t answer using the usual axioms or  rules that you’re allowed to use normally,   but sometimes we add new rules. There are other  foundations of mathematics which can prove more   things than the standard ones. Sometimes we do  play with different rules, like when you play   chess. There are some standard rules of chess,  but sometimes we also consider other variants. We’ve moved to a more pluralistic view  of mathematics, where there isn’t just   one true mathematics and one universal true  and false facts. There is a standard one,   but we do also consider more exotic alternate  types of mathematics, where we have more rules   or fewer rules, and there’s a multiverse of  different types of mathematics to play with.   We have different number systems.  We have different geometries. Mathematics has evolved over time to just a more  pluralistic view of everything. We are comfortable   with it now, but it was a very uneasy feeling to  discover this result in 1930, that your worldview   of mathematics changed. It’s as if you thought the  Earth was stationary, and now you know it moves. COWEN: Is it fair to say your overall  approach to the foundations of math is   quite pragmatic? It’s not Hilbert,  it’s not Brouwer. There’s really   no result that could come along that  would make you feel nihilistic. It’s   just there’s different avenues to explore  things. Is your view different than that? TAO: Yes. I try to have some humility. There  are certain mathematical models that I like,   and I think they explain the real world.  There have been revolutions in the past   where quantum mechanics, you mentioned, was a  very big philosophical transition in physics.   We are currently going through a transition  where most of mathematics was human-generated,   and we’re now entering an era where  proofs are being generated by AI. This is also changing our philosophical  foundations of what does it mean to prove   something. What does it mean to understand  something? As I said, these two statements   used to be almost synonymous, and now they have  been decoupled quite severely. I try to keep an   open mind, which I think is part of what it  means to be a good scientist. You don’t have   a dogmatic view of what science is or isn’t.  You update it based on events and new data. COWEN: How much do you read in the earlier  history of mathematics, say, 19th century,   early 20th century? Do you learn by doing that,  or it’s just a fun thing you do as a hobby? TAO: I think mathematics is about stories a  lot more than is normally presented. If you   take a math class, maybe you might hear some  stories about there was a mathematician called   Évariste Galois, who died in a duel. He was  writing very frantically the basis of what   we now call Galois theory the night before the  duel because he was certain he was going to die,   and he did. There are lots of wonderful  stories that make the subject come alive. Unfortunately, often when you present them  in classes, you take out all the backstory   and the side context, often because of lack of  time. There’s a lot of math that you want to   give to your students. Math often comes across as  just a bunch of equations and rules and recipes.   I do find that reading the histories makes  it come alive. There are some really good   stories in the history of mathematics, which,  luckily, they make for great podcast stories   and YouTube videos. Maybe they do get heard  by the public, but not in classrooms so much. COWEN: How much of abstract mathematics do  you feel is useful? Is it like a lottery   ticket where maybe one in every 200 things  is useful, but it’s clearly worth doing,   or is your view that if we knew everything,  explored all angles, it would all fit together,   and every part of it would be a unified  whole that could be used for something? TAO: Right. I view STEM as a whole—science,  technology, engineering, and mathematics—as   an ecosystem, and mathematics is the soil. It’s at  the foundations. It doesn’t generate the fruits,   the things that are most directly useful for  humans, but it sets the stage. Of course,   it gives us all the formulas and recipes that  other scientists use. It also sets limits.   Most other sciences or engineering, they tell  you what’s possible. You can build a rocket,   and it flies, and now you’ve proven  that it is possible for a rocket to fly. If you want to show that something’s impossible,  that there's a limit, for example, if you want to   communicate using a wireless spectrum, what is  the maximum amount of bits you can stream from   A to B? There’s a branch of mathematics,  information theory, that tells you this, and   it gives you limits. There’s a maximum theoretical  limit, and you can’t discover this by engineering. You can send more and more bits down a channel,   but only mathematics can tell you that there’s  a limit. This is useful because it tells you   how close you are to perfection, and when  to stop trying to develop an even better   wireless encoding protocol because you’re  already at 98 percent of mathematical capacity.   There’s really no point to spend another  $1 million trying to make it any better. Mathematics unifies science.  It gives a common language,   so scientists get to talk to other  scientists. Whether something’s useful   or not, it often takes decades. Shannon’s  information theory came out in the ’40s,   but it’s only when cellphones came along and  big data that it really became so essential   to the modern economy. Even if a topic is  useless now, who knows in 20 years, 40 years. COWEN: When string theory is presented to you,  viewing it just as a mathematician, does it feel   beautiful to you, or do you think this is strange  and awkward, it’s not intuitive enough? What’s   this higher number of dimensions doing here?  Is it interesting math to you? What is it? TAO: This is less of my field. The  ideas from string theory have impacted   geometry quite a lot. The modern field of  mathematical geometry already studies very   high-dimensional objects and making them even  higher dimensional by turning points into little   strings, they’re very comfortable with that.  My understanding is that the ideas proposed   by physicists have inspired mathematicians to  solve many geometry problems in their own field. Now, my understanding also—I’m not really a  physicist, though—is that while the theory   is very beautiful, it could have been a good  explanation of the real world, but we have   not found a really striking confirmation that  string theory really is a good model. One of the   objections that I’ve heard is that it’s actually  too flexible a theory. There are too many ways   in which these strings can vibrate. While they  can explain our current universe, they can also   explain trillions and trillions of other alternate  universes, and there’s no obvious way to explain   why we live in this one and not in all the other  universes that are compatible with string theory. I don’t know to what extent string theory  is still the leading proposal for, say,   quantum gravity, which is one of the  big goals of modern theoretical physics,   to unify quantum mechanics and gravity.  There was a lot of hope that string theory   would do this. They’ve tried for many decades.  I think that there’s still no really conclusive   evidence that it’s working. I think people  are beginning to explore other alternatives   to string theory as well, but you may have to  talk to a physicist for the latest on that. COWEN: Reading your book, I  come away with the gut feeling,   a purely subjective impression, but that  you love geometry most. Is that justified? TAO: I love all kinds of mathematics. Maybe I like   it because I’m not as good at it  as with other types of mathematics.   There are mathematicians who are very visual, and  they can see a complicated shape and rotate it in   their mind. I can’t do that. I actually have to  write things out and use visual aids, blackboards,   to really see geometry. I have to put some  real effort to understand geometric ideas.   Maybe because of that effort, the ones that I  do understand, I actually find quite beautiful. My native field is actually more analysis.  I like understanding what things are big,   what things are small. If you add a  whole bunch of small things together,   can you get something big? When  do waves interfere constructively,   destructively? That type of mathematics feels very  natural to me. I try to appreciate all kinds of   mathematics. I’ve learned a lot by talking to  fellow colleagues who think about mathematics   in a different way. I’ve learned a lot from them,  and hopefully, they’ve learned something from me. COWEN: With respect to real analysis,  why does that come so relatively late   in the history of math? It doesn’t seem that  difficult in a way, once it occurs to you,   that there’s such a thing at all, even  if some of the results are difficult. TAO: Traditionally, mathematics was about  exact formulas and numbers: 2 + 3 is exactly 5.   It’s only when we started dealing with really  large quantities, like astronomical scales of   numbers or big data, whatever, that we  needed to start working approximately.   If you want to know the GDP of the United  States, you don’t need it for the nearest penny.   Just getting the first few digits is enough.  It took a while to figure out what was the   mathematics for orders of magnitude, and  I talked about what happens in the limit. If instead of working in a family of  five people or a village of 100 people,   you work with hundreds of millions of people,  you actually really want to send the number   of people off to infinity and ask, what is going  on in the infinite limit? Often, the mathematics   becomes simpler. It’s like if you want to  model a whole bunch of particles of a fluid,   you could model all the trillions of particles  bouncing around, but actually, it’s easier to   think of it as a continuous object and talk about  pressure and volume and macroscopic quantities. Early mathematicians struggled a  lot with infinity. The Greeks had   all these paradoxes. They didn’t understand how  infinity worked. It was a very nontrivial task.   It took centuries to work out how to  deal with infinity safely. It’s like   radioactive material. Not all the laws of  algebra work with infinity. It really has   to be handled with care, but it is very  powerful once you know how to use it. COWEN: Zero as a number, that seems to come,   in a way, late in mathematics. That’s  what, the 7th century AD in India? TAO: Yes. COWEN: Zero seems so simple to  us. Why does that take so long? TAO: Because it’s invisible. I think it’s human  nature to only give names to things that you   see. You see a sheep, that’s a sheep. You see  two sheep, that’s two sheep. You see nothing,   you don’t say, “I see zero sheep.” It is a  conceptual leap. It requires some abstraction.   People inferred the need for zero by manipulating  the numbers that they could see. In fact, I think   there are many languages where they don’t even  have a name for one. The counting system starts   at two. Even the idea that a single object you  can attach a count, one, to it, that’s already a   conceptual leap. You may think that if you see  a sheep, you don’t need to call it one sheep. People had to work with numbers of two, three,  four, five, and they started applying rules to   these numbers. They discovered addition and  subtraction and other arithmetic operations.   Just by following the rules of what  these operations were trying to do,   they were naturally led to consider new  numbers: one, zero, negative numbers, fractions,   square roots. These are numbers that are not  obvious. You can’t see −3 sheep or √2 sheep. Once you trust in the laws of arithmetic, and you  just accept that they are predicting other numbers   to exist and be useful, then we found them. Now  we teach them in our primary school classes,   so it’s obvious to us. We’ve internalized  things like zero. It was a major conceptual   breakthrough back in the 7th century,  as you say. We shouldn’t mock these   ancient mathematicians for  not knowing what zero was. COWEN: When you look at mathematical economics  over the last two decades, is it interesting to   you as math, or is it just a bunch of people doing  something different that, to you, is low level? TAO: Oh, yes, I was always fascinated by  economics. I love game theory, and actually often   there are pure math problems where it’s actually  good to think in game theory terms. In analysis,   you have all these complicated statements, like  for every ε, there exists a δ, blah, blah, blah.   It looks very intimidating, but if you phrase it  as a game, your opponent is giving you an ε, you   need to counter that ε with a δ of your own. If  you view it as a game, then actually you can talk   about strategies and who’s ahead, who’s behind. It  actually activates really good modes of thinking. I’ve used economic thinking in my own  work. We talk about cost functions and   minimizing loss. There are lots of concepts.  Ricardo’s law of comparative advantage,   I use that to run my life. There are so  many things I can do. What do I choose   to spend my time on? It’s actually a very  useful principle: comparative advantage. Economics, I find it’s a very good arena to  understand the difference between models and   reality. Physics, we’re spoiled because  we’ve had these great physicists who’ve   created these very accurate models of the real  world, classical mechanics, quantum mechanics,   and they’re very well tested and very  accurate. You can just go to town exploring   their consequences and still predict reality.  Economics is a much more mixed situation where   you have models, and sometimes they predict the  real world very well, but sometimes they don’t. In addition to doing the math, you also have  to do the modeling, and you have to understand   the limits of when a model starts breaking  down and what you need to do to adjust it.   I find that fascinating. It’s somewhere between  the hard sciences and the social sciences. There’s   enough hard models that you can do math, but  there’s also enough real-world messiness that you   have to also grapple with the subjectivity. As an  outsider, I find it a really fascinating subject. COWEN: When you looked at the Black-Scholes model,   were you shocked when the probability  doesn’t matter? Was that beautiful to you? TAO: Yes, yes, yes. There is a special feature of  Gaussian fluctuations that you can price options   just by knowing risk. There is one algebraic  miracle that makes this work. Normally,   predicting future costs of anything  is just an intractable problem,   and there just happens to be this miracle.  If you have Gaussian fluctuations,   then it is beautiful. This is actually a  really good example of when you need to   know when the models work and when they don’t  work. If you don’t have Gaussian fluctuations,   then actually Black-Scholes is somewhat dangerous  to use, especially if you compound it into   derivatives over and over again. Again, that’s  an old story. You know what happened in 2009. COWEN: Nick Bostrom has a famous argument using  Bayesian analysis that probably we’re living in   a simulation. I’m not sure if he believes it, but  he doesn’t reject it. When you hear that argument,   are you, A, convinced, or B, you think  it’s somehow a misuse of mathematics? TAO: I think it’s a good attempt. Bayesian  reasoning is very subtle because, as I said,   it’s already hard enough dealing with a  model because you don’t know whether the   model is accurate or not accurate. Bayesian  reasoning, you’re not just dealing with one   model of the world, but you’re dealing  with multiple models of the world,   and you have some prior belief as to how likely  each model is, and then you’re updating them. It could be that you may be considering  two models, let’s say a hypothesis and   a null hypothesis, but there could be a third  hypothesis that you’re not considering at all,   which is actually the true explanation. If you  focus only on the two hypotheses that you can   think of, maybe it’s your lack of imagination,  which is actually blocking you from seeing the   real truth. You have to be aware of your own  limitations when you do Bayesian reasoning. That said, you can use some reasoning like this.  There are certain models for the universe that   you can refute by pure reasoning. In ancient  times, people believed in prophecy and fate,   that certain people were destined to  have something happen 20 years from now,   but this is very incompatible with free will and  having laws of nature that are very predictable.   It’s also incompatible, to some extent, to being  in a simulation, for instance. You can do these   thought experiments, and you can play off various  grand philosophical ideas against each other.   You can play off the idea of simulation  against the idea of there being a creator. One amusing thing I saw on  the internet recently is that   the fact that we can now create AIs that  appear smarter than us has theological   implications as to how intelligent  our creator was compared to ourselves. COWEN: Yes. TAO: It is entertaining to explore these  thought experiments, but you do have to be   very humble that we could be limited by our  own imagination. We are comparing different   models to explain the universe, but there  are infinitely many other models that could   also explain things and sometimes  we are just completely off track. COWEN: Newcomb’s paradox. Are you a one-boxer or  a two-boxer? You sound like a one-boxer so far. TAO: Oh, okay. I have to be reminded— COWEN: That’s the Nozick problem from  the—well, it comes from Newcomb, of course,   but you can grab one box or two box, and  you’re told by a potentially omniscient   being that if you grab both boxes, you’ll end  up with less. The dominance principle tells   you to take both boxes. Expected utility  maximization says only take the one box. TAO: Right. One thing that this paradox shows  you is that sometimes having more free will and   agency actually hurts you. You may think that the  more optionality and ability to think you have,   the better you’ll be off in life. That seems  intuitive. As I recall of Newcomb’s paradox,   if you lobotomize yourself to say, “I will  actually do surgery on my brain so that I cannot   take two boxes, I will only be able to take  one box,” then this being that is observing   you will see that, and it will reward  you. Whereas if you’re overthinking it,   then you may actually get penalized. Newcomb’s paradox is actually an environment  where you are penalized for thinking too   much. It’s an exception to the rule that  being more rational is an advantage. It   is a nice thought experiment, but it may  have real-world implications. There are   actually some scenarios where you don’t  want to signal that you’re too smart. COWEN: David Lewis has this famous article,  I think it’s 1982, where he argues the   repeated prisoner’s dilemma is a lot like  Newcomb’s paradox. This is a contested claim. TAO: I can see that, yes. Actually, I saw a great  talk about this recently, that if you automate   your prisoner’s dilemma strategy with a computer  program and everyone gets to see your computer   program—it’s a very simple strategy, like maybe  you cooperate unless you saw someone defect, and   then you defect yourself. If you signal in advance  what you do and you remove your own free will,   then you can actually do better in the game  because people will see that you’re trusted. There was this debate about a year ago: If you’re  a woman, would you rather be with a man or a bear?   Many women said they feel safer with a bear,  and I think one of the reasons is that the bear   has a much higher rationality. It’s much more  predictable what the bear will do, and the fact   that interacting with someone who is really  intelligent actually adds risk. There’s lots   of games like that. I think the game of chicken  is another game where one of the strategies to   win chicken is to actually disable your steering  wheel and just go full speed ahead, but visibly   throw away your steering wheel. Then the rational  strategy for the other player is to swerve. COWEN: Let’s say we put you in charge  of math education in the United States.   Put aside AI. We’ll get to that in a bit.  How would you improve math education here? TAO: Oh, that is a really complex problem.  My main experience with education is at the   university level. I’m at a fairly prestigious  university where we are quite selective,   so we get among the best students coming  from both the American and overseas high   schools. I don’t have the best view of what’s  going on at the K-12 level. I talk to people,   and I have two kids who have gone through the K-12  system, but that’s really a small amount of data. COWEN: Wasn’t there a recent report  that UCLA faculty complained that a   lot of the entering students didn’t even  have great middle school math? Some do,   some are excellent. I’ve taught in  the UC system, but it’s high variance. TAO: Yes. There was a report from UC San  Diego in particular that was quite concerning   about the basic readiness of many of the  students. I’m not sure whether it’s because our   selection system needs fixing. There’s  a debate to reinstate the SAT in the UC.   Or whether it’s because of COVID. That could be  a consequence. Some people say that social media   has destroyed the attention spans of school  kids. We don’t know. There are people who try   to systematically study education quantitatively  and try to see what types of pedagogy work best,   but it is a very soft science. I think  some of the findings are controversial. I do think we need lots of experiments, and  some way to scale up experiments that work   on a single school to the whole system. I do know  that there have been lots of little experiments.   Let’s flip the classes. Let’s ban technology, or  let’s do things in a different way. When you do   it on a small scale, it can be great. When you  have some teachers who are really enthusiastic   about this experiment and the kids are excited  about trying something new, you can get these   fantastic results. Then you try to deploy them  to 100 schools, and suddenly it doesn’t work. One big issue is getting from a prototype  experiment to a large-scale deployment.   This I don’t know how to solve.  There’s some pragmatic realities of   just how education works at a typical,  let’s say, American high school, that   you can’t ignore just because something  works in some nice lab school experiment. COWEN: Many of my economist friends, they think   we should teach less trigonometry  and more statistics. Do you agree? TAO: Yes, I think that is a tweak. Traditionally,  the college math syllabus consists of a lot of   calculus, because for the classic applications  to physics and engineering and the hard sciences,   calculus was almost the most important  higher math skill that you needed.   In the era of big data, statistics  and now machine learning and linear   algebra and probability are becoming more  important. We are making some tweaks there. Although mathematics is often not about  the specific tools that you learn,   but just how to deal with abstract  situations and how to problem-solve.   I view math as a good playground to think where  the cost of failure is cheap. In the real world,   if you do something in the real world and you make  a mistake, it could be very expensive. If you’re a   civil engineer and you’re tasked to build a bridge  and you make a mistake and the bridge collapses,   you made a very expensive mistake. If you’re  a surgeon and you cut the wrong thing,   you’ve made a very fatal mistake, perhaps. If you  have a math problem and you solve it incorrectly,   you just have wasted half an hour of your  time, but you can go back and do it again. The specific tools you learn in math are somewhat  useful, but actually just the ability to play and   try to solve problems when there’s some unknowns  and things you don’t understand. How do you even   start? How do you set up the model? How do you not  get terrified of all the possibilities, and how to   not get paralyzed when you’re faced with anything  complex. That, I think, is the valuable skill, the   most valuable. All the other stuff you can look up  or even consult an AI now if you really wanted to. COWEN: You did a math Olympiad  when you were 10. Should there   be some kind of embedded calculus option  in 7th grade that, if you want to do it,   you can just learn calculus early on, and if  kids don’t want to do it, they don’t have to? TAO: There are Advanced Placement-type exams,  and there are math enrichment. There’s math   clubs. I think it’s good to have a lot of options  like this. They shouldn’t be mandatory. I think   if a kid doesn’t want to do these  things and you push them into this,   they will just have a horrible  time and end up hating mathematics. Whether you want to formally include  this in the standard school system,   I think there could be special schools where they  have experts, and they really make an effort to   integrate these competitions and nonstandard  classes into their framework. It can work,   I think, when there is the supporting  infrastructure—so qualified teachers,   supportive administration, and just general  rules for how a student can choose these   activities in place of standard classes,  but it may not scale to the average school. There may not be enough qualified teachers. Some  schools may have policies that are just somehow   not compatible. There may be too many parents  in one school that just do not like this type   of education. I think these options should exist,  and it should be possible for parents and kids   to select among several school options, some of  which would offer these and some of which don’t. COWEN: How do you feel about quant finance?  Do you view it as a brain drain out of math,   or the potentially high wages overall attract  more talent into math, and some of the people   still end up doing things in mathematics, so the  net effect on math is positive? What’s your view? TAO: On the one hand, mathematics,  like academia in general, we don’t   have enough positions in academia. Academia is  a fairly small sector of the economy. We train   many more students than can end up having  academic jobs. As a very practical matter,   we need other industries that also value  mathematicians and can hire people with, say,   math PhDs. Quantitative finance has been very  good at that, so often they actually pay very,   very well, better than academics  in many cases. I think that’s fine. There are many positive uses of quantitative  finance. Used properly, you can price things well,   you can get accurate market signals, you can  get liquidity. If you pursue the wrong metrics   too much, you can also destabilize economies  and create crashes. It impacts the real world,   so you have to be more aware of these issues  than if you were just a pure mathematician. There have been mathematicians who were very  successful in finance and gave back to the   math community. Jim Simons is one example. He  founded Renaissance Technologies. He made many,   many billions of dollars, and actually, he  founded the Simons Foundation, which is now   a major sponsor of pure mathematics and physics  and astronomy and computer science. It works out. I do think academics do need to get out of the  ivory tower sometimes and engage with various   industries—finance, the tech industry. Here  at UCLA, we’re close to Hollywood, we had a   lot of ties with computer graphics industries,  for instance, and the movie industry. There are   many sectors of the economy now which are  becoming more mathematized. They need people   with good math skills, and we should  engage with all of them, I think. COWEN: How long do you think it will  be before AIs create the equivalent of   new Millennium Problems for mathematics? Is that  two years away, 20 years away? Interesting ones. TAO: It’s extremely uncertain times  now. I think a lot of assumptions   about how mathematics operates is going  to change a lot. There’s so many changes,   but in one sentence, we have moved from an  era of proof scarcity to proof abundance. It used to be that proofs were really hard  and valuable, and so we would create these   open problems as these goals, these  landmarks, and we would march toward   these goals very slowly and deliberately, but  we’d pick up all these insights and techniques   and learn all these things along the way.  We have these Millennium Prize Problems,   and we have these targets that guided us, but  they’re relatively few in number. There’s only   seven Millennium Prize Problems. That was the  way things worked in a proof-scarcity era. I think going forward, the idea of  focusing on individual problems,   that currency has basically been hyperinflated.  We now have machines that can just brute-force,   basically solve massive numbers of the old  problems that we used to use as landmarks,   and we have to really switch to some sort  of math 2.0. I think instead of dealing with   individual problems, we may start creating  huge datasets of thousands or millions of   problems and try to sweep them out. With this  AI, I can handle 30 percent of these problems.   Using this idea that this human contributed,  I can solve this 10 percent, but not pick out   individual problems per se anymore as the  goals, but work at a much higher scale. I think that it will take a lot of cultural  shift. We are not used to mass production of   mathematics. We are still, in many  ways, in a pre-industrial economy,   math academia. We are forced, almost  at gunpoint right now, to switch to   an industrial or post-industrial economy, and  this will take quite a bit of cultural change,   but I think that’s what’s going to happen.  Individual problems, even like Millennium-level,   may disappear, and we will just have lots  and lots of big datasets of problems. COWEN: On net, you’re happy? Unhappy? TAO: That’s not the right word. It’s very  complicated. I’m excited by the possibility   of completely new types of mathematics  that didn’t exist before, but I’m also   actually quite horrified by the disruption,  which I think was much more than necessary. Of course, every revolution, like the Industrial  Revolution, of course, is a famous example,   it creates job displacement and so forth. I  think there was some medium between status quo   and transition to a new paradigm where you had  more of the benefits of transition and fewer of   the disruptions. If the Industrial Revolution  happened within one month, it would have been   much more traumatic, entire careers cut short  with no ability to transition halfway through. COWEN: It would have been better overall,   right? Like our standard of living,  people might have had in the 1950s.   TAO: Yes, but a lot might have been destroyed  permanently. There are still pre-industrial ways   of handcrafting certain objects or doing things  in a very old-school way. There are communities   that keep these more artisanal types of craft  alive, and they have cultural value. There was   enough time in the revolution to preserve these  culturally significant artifacts. It is possible   that there could be some major disaster where  we lose our power grid or something, and some of   these antiquated skills actually become relevant  again. Actually, from a strategic point of view,   there’s actually some value in preserving  what you might think of as obsolete skills. Sometimes the historical insights of how an  obsolete practice developed can inform the   development of a modern skill. We talked about  the importance of history and mathematics. It’s   true. History is important everywhere. If you rush  the transition too much and you just focus on just   getting your productivity up or hitting some other  benchmark, you may lose some of this less tangible   value that you may only see after the fact what  you’ve lost. It’s like everything. If you want   to do urban development, you need to tear  down old buildings to create new ones, but   some buildings have actual historical value,  and there is a way to develop sustainably. COWEN: Will the individual paper  still be the research unit for   human mathematicians, or will that change also? TAO: I believe that will change, especially  since now AIs can generate that unit at a press   of a button. First of all, that unit used  to be bundled with other valuable things.   Traditionally, when a mathematician created  a paper, they also created a skilled author   who could then give talks about that  paper. They could go to conferences,   they could interact with other humans,  they could train students. Through that,   they can discover new connections, new  collaborations, new questions to ask. Now we have these AIs that generate the  paper, but without all that extra value.   They have unbundled the PDF, the actual  physical paper, from the penumbra of more social   or intangible values of that paper. Also,  when a human solves those and writes a paper,   it came from first understanding the  problem and getting some insights,   and that you can communicate. The AI often  does not communicate what it learned when it   solves the problem. It just gives you the  output, but the process is very opaque. On the one hand, I think papers will evolve  to show much more of the process. We have   focused a bit too much in the past on just showing  the finished product, but we’ve seen it in other   disciplines. Movies are enriched when you see  behind-the-scenes documentaries and lots of   extra material. People enjoy that extra content,  and I think papers will move in that direction. I also think that we will also work at much  larger scales than papers. We will see entire   databases which are like the equivalent  of thousands of papers networked together   in a single spreadsheet, which you can  query and you can update in real time,   and you can get all these visualizations, which  you just could not do with the old system. Or   every time you wanted a new way to visualize the  literature, someone has to write a new paper, and   you have to wait a year before you get a different  view. You should be able to see an entire field. I think people will have to move to more  collaborative, big math projects. Instead of   a small number of people working on individual  papers and then contributing atomically to   the literature, the literature itself  would be a much more networked, living,   collaborative entity where both AIs and humans can  collaborate. I think this is the only way forward. We’ve seen in recent months that brute  competition between humans and AIs is   becoming very counterproductive. People  are just racing to dump out a paper three   minutes before someone else with an AI is  generating almost exactly the same paper,   and everyone is cutting corners and making the  papers harder and harder to read just because   they want the priority. Priority used to be a  very good way to organize our field and encourage   people to produce results in a timely fashion.  The metric has become way too over-optimized now,   and we need to switch, as you say, to beyond  thinking at the scale of a single paper. COWEN: Now, you had started a new “journal,” if  that’s the right word, where people submit video   talks rather than printed papers. Does that  now become more important or less important? TAO: I believe exposition, in general,  has been undervalued in mathematics. We   used to let the papers speak for themselves.  Proofs were scarce, and there were few enough   difficult papers that it worked that, when  a new result came out that was interesting,   everyone dropped what they were doing and read  those papers. Now, the flood of papers coming out,   in every field, there are 10 times, 100 times  more interesting papers than people can read. The bottleneck is now, what are the results  that can be explained human to human? Papers are   actually a very terrible way to communicate. Most  people have not had the experience of reading an   academic paper, but it’s much easier if you can  interact with a human expert and ask questions,   use body language, use some visual aids.  Talks have been one of the traditional ways   in which we do that. We view these as secondary  byproducts of research, but I think, increasingly,   they will become one of the primary outputs,  especially since papers can be generated now   by AIs. Having the human-to-human  experience is increasingly valuable. COWEN: Just for our last segment,   a few questions about you. What is  your favorite Hong Kong action movie? TAO: Ha. It’s this half action movie, half comedy.  My favorite is called Kung Fu Hustle by Stephen   Chow. It came out about 20 years ago, back in the  golden age of Hong Kong cinema. I’ve not really   followed the modern era, but it is hilarious. It’s  an over-the-top parody of Hong Kong action movies.   The fights become more and more ridiculous  and absurd, but also just incredibly funny.   It works best in the original Cantonese, but it  holds up in English. I recommend it to everybody. COWEN: I like Drunken Master II, with  Jackie Chan. Do you know that one? TAO: Yes, I watched it when I was a kid. COWEN: Sometimes it’s retitled as just  Drunken Master. You have to be careful   with the edition because the first  Drunken Master is not that good. TAO: Yes. The conceit is that he’s  a martial artist who becomes better   the more drunk he is. There’s this very  weird style. This is very typical golden   age Hong Kong action cinema. You  start with some ridiculous conceit,   and you just run with it, and you just play  it straight. That’s also a very good one. COWEN: What do you find most beautiful in music? TAO: I used to enjoy classical music when I was a  kid, especially Bach, the very intricate patterns.   Nowadays, sometimes I like epic instrumental  music, like the Lord of the Rings soundtrack or   something. Sometimes it inspires me into a working  mood. Sometimes I just need some random pop music   that is very familiar as comfort, some Taylor  Swift thing or something, something mindless. Actually, it’s funny. I have access now. I can  play any piece of music now just by searching   on the internet very quickly. I actually listen  to it a lot less than when I had to have CDs and   things. It’s interesting. The more abundant  something is, sometimes the less you use it. COWEN: Now, as an undergraduate,   you went to Flinders University in  Adelaide. That’s correct, in Australia? TAO: Yes. COWEN: Do you feel you somehow would have  done worse had you gone to Cambridge or   Princeton? Is it part of your success  that you had this unusual beginning? TAO: Yes. My parents worked very hard to design an  education track that suited me. I skipped a lot of   grades. In fact, in math and science, I skipped  five grades. Emotionally and in the humanities,   I was not at that level, so I would also take  classes in physical education and English in   my regular year. I had this very complicated  schedule where, when I was in primary school,   I would take some classes in high school. When  I was in high school, I’d take math classes   at university. I enrolled in university at the  age of 13, I think, but I still lived at home. Flinders University was a small university, but  it was a short drive from where we lived. I knew   all the faculty, and we were in small classes.  There was a particular math professor where we met   every week just for an hour, just talking math,  very casually. I took my classes, and actually,   I even failed some. I wasn’t actually the best  student, to be honest, but it was at my level. COWEN: This is in math you failed some? TAO: Yes, yes. Actually, quantum mechanics is also  a class that I failed. The two classes I failed   were Introduction to Fortran. I liked programming  in BASIC. I didn’t want to switch to Fortran, so I   refused to learn Fortran, and I failed the class.  Then Introduction to Quantum Mechanics, where the   class was half solving differential equations, and  that was fine, I liked doing the math, and half   explaining the history of quantum mechanics. There  was an essay component, and I just refused to do   the essay, and I failed. I remember crying. I  actually had to be escorted out of the exam room. I think actually not being in a super  competitive environment at the time,   but in a small place where everyone knew everyone  else, I felt on par with my other students, that   worked well for me. Then I went to Princeton as a  graduate student, and that was a much more elite   institution. I was shocked at how much my fellow  grad students knew a lot more math than I did.   It was in grad school that I failed the first  exam that I really did not expect to fail. I failed two exams when I was an undergraduate,  but these were classes I didn’t care about,   and I expected to do badly. My qualifying exam  was an oral exam, and I actually learned I was   terrible at oral exams. I could not convince my  adviser that I knew the subject I was studying,   and he was very disappointed with me.  It actually changed my life. I actually   started studying it much harder and actually  putting real effort into explaining what I do.   I tried not to disappoint my adviser  ever again. It worked out for me. COWEN: That’s quite an unusual  history. Today or more recently,   what’s your most unusual successful work habit? TAO: I am learning the power of  delegation more and more now. I   used to want to do everything myself, but I  am finding that my research collaborations,   trusting the junior people to take the  lead, working with students. Nowadays,   with the internet and AI, AI in particular,  it can be a very dehumanizing technology,   but it can also be a very empowering technology.  It can enable junior people to take the lead in   projects where traditionally only senior people  had the experience to handle complex tasks. I’m finding that people rise to the challenge,  that if you give someone an ambitious task,   and they’re bright and they’re motivated, they  often can exceed your expectations and do things   that you wouldn’t have thought of. I have a blog  where, for almost the entire history of the blog,   I wrote like 99 percent of the articles.  Recently, I’ve turned over my blog to the   community, and now 95 percent of the  articles are written by other people,   and actually they’re great. They offer points  of view that I would not have thought of. COWEN: How do you think about your own  level of stamina? I don’t know your age,   but you’re not 23 anymore, and you’re  still doing plenty and then some, right? TAO: Yes. I’m 51 now, and yes, I am exhausted  quite a lot. This is another reason why I’m   learning to delegate. I have no choice. Delegating  to humans, also delegating to AI some things. I   am learning that you can’t do everything  yourself. Sometimes you just accept that   other people can do things better than you can.  Every morning of my day, I’m doing something,   but it’s something I choose to do, and I feel  good about it, even though I’m always tired. COWEN: Very last topic, a very simple one.  Collatz conjecture: Is it true or false? TAO: It’s true, but we have no idea how  to prove it, even with our fancy AIs.   The Collatz conjecture is sometimes called  the hailstone conjecture. You take a number.   If it’s odd, you make it bigger, you  multiply by 3 and add 1. If it’s even,   you make it smaller, you divide by 2. Then  you just iterate this over and over again,   and the numbers go bouncing up and  down like a hailstone. With hail,   every hailstone eventually lands and goes down to  Earth, and we think the same is true with Collatz,   that every number, it goes up and down, but it  will eventually hit 1, no matter what you do. The first trillion numbers we’ve  tested do this. We also now know that,   in some sense, almost all numbers either  do this or come very close to this. We’ve   made some statistical progress on this conjecture,   but there’s always a chance that there’s this  one very special hailstone that just somehow,   instead of falling to Earth, just keeps floating  up and up, higher and higher, or maybe in a loop. There could be one special exception or a  small number of exceptions, and we can’t   rule this out. It’s like if you’re at  a casino and you keep playing roulette,   most of the time you will lose because  the odds are in the casino’s favor. There   could be one special scenario where you  just keep winning over and over again,   and you just get richer and richer. Of course,  at some point, the casino will kick you out.   For Collatz, we can’t rule out that one  exceptionally lucky hailstone. None of   the ideas we have in mathematics come close to  ruling out this very extra special conspiracy.   I would love to know how to do that, but I don’t  think I’ll see that in my lifetime, even with AI. COWEN: Just to plug your book again, Six Math  Essentials. Terry Tao, thank you very much. TAO: Thank you for having me.

transcript_segments.text: TYLER COWEN: Hello, everyone, and welcome  back to Conversations with Tyler. Today,
I’m very happy to be speaking with Terry  Tao. He has a new and excellent book out,
Six Math Essentials. Terry is arguably the  greatest mathematician of his generation.
He is a Fields Medal winner, a professor  of mathematics at UCLA, and he has done
research in topics as varied as harmonic  analysis, partial differential equations,
algebraic combinatorics, arithmetic combinatorics,  geometric combinatorics, probability theory,
compressed sensing, analytic number theory, and  he writes a blog, and much more. Terry, welcome.
TERENCE TAO: Oh, pleasure to be here.
COWEN: Now, people often think  of mathematics as about logic,
but I’d like to start by asking you about  emotions. I’ll name a few results in math,
and you tell me what emotions  they evoke in you, okay?
TAO: All right.
COWEN: Euler’s identity.
TAO: That is a very pretty and neat identity.  It connects all the fundamental constants of
mathematics: e, π, i, and 1 and 0. Actually,  to me, what is most beautiful about it is that
what it’s really saying is that rotation  is actually a type of multiplication.
Euler’s formula, you can think of it as eiπ  = −1. This is one form of Euler’s formula.
When you exponentiate, raise e to something,  it’s like you’re multiplying something over
and over again. Compound interest is one  place where exponentiation shows up. The i
shifts things from just multiplying to  make things bigger or smaller, but instead,
we’re multiplying at right angles and making  it rotating. eiπ is saying that if you rotate
something by π, π radians, you flip it. It  becomes the negative of what you start with.
It actually connects geometry and dynamics  and algebra. It’s a very beautiful formula.
COWEN: When you ponder quantum  mechanics, what do you feel?
TAO: Oh, yes.
COWEN: For me, it’s puzzlement,  but you’re smarter than I am.
TAO: It uses very abstract mathematics,  the mathematics of Hilbert spaces,
which are these infinite-dimensional vector  spaces, and complex numbers. You definitely
need a fair bit of mathematical training to  understand the mathematics. It also forces you to
really change your idea of what reality is.  It’s like how we used to think that the Earth
was stationary, and then we had to change  our perspective and think of the Earth as
moving. Before quantum mechanics, we  used to think of physical objects as
always only being in one state. A light  is on or off. The cat is alive or dead.
In order for the equations of quantum mechanics  to work, you have to accept that, in fact,
most of the time, objects live in superpositions.  A cat is neither alive nor dead, but a mixture of
both. They interact with each other in funny  ways, like how waves can interfere with each
other. It is a very unintuitive way  of thinking about reality because we
don’t see ourselves in superpositions, but the  math actually works out. Despite everything,
it actually is a better way  of explaining the world,
especially at a molecular level. It is very  mysterious, and it was very controversial when
it first came out. A lot of physicists did  not accept what the math was telling them.
COWEN: The Riemann hypothesis, what do you feel?
TAO: Oh, yes. That is a really big prize in  mathematics. Actually, recently we’re getting
some progress on that. That’s another story.  It concerns one of the most basic objects in
mathematics, the prime numbers, which we  now use prime numbers all over the place,
like in cryptography. For instance, a lot of  cryptographic protocols that we use to encrypt
our finances and whatever rely on properties of  the prime numbers. We look at the prime numbers,
and they behave very randomly. Sometimes they’re  close together, sometimes they’re far apart.
The Riemann hypothesis is a very precise way  of quantifying this random-looking nature of
the primes, and it has many, many consequences.  Any part of mathematics that touches the primes,
if you know the Riemann hypothesis,  normally your results get stronger.
There’s a large chunk of results in number  theory which are conditional. If you have
the Riemann hypothesis, you get this good  result. Otherwise, we can’t say anything.
Out of all the results, open questions in  mathematics, most open questions in mathematics,
they’re like puzzles. We don’t solve them for  their own sake. They’re useful for gaining
insight and help us eventually understand more  realistic, real-world problems. The Riemann
hypothesis is one of the few mathematical  questions which is actually quite useful
for its own sake. Knowing that it’s true  would actually imply a lot of other things.
COWEN: You think it will be proven, can be proven?
TAO: We are making progress.  In fact, just two days ago,
there was a significant advance on the Riemann  hypothesis. We are still quite a ways from the
full resolution, but now there are new ideas.  Unfortunately, the ideas were generated by AI,
and we don’t yet understand them. This is  part of the new era now. We are getting
answers without understanding, which  is a very strange era to be in.
Historically, the only way to make a progress  on a difficult mathematical problem was to
understand it, and you could communicate these  insights to others. Now we have these machines
that can give us answers, but we have to  really work much harder than normal to
extract out the useful insights from them. It  is a strange era. We now have these new tools,
and hopefully we will have lots of mathematicians  exploring both old methods and new methods,
and we will find something. It  will probably require a new idea
which we haven’t seen before. We know the  limits of many of the existing techniques.
COWEN: Gödel’s incompleteness  theorem, does it frustrate you?
TAO: Yes. Mathematics is going through a crisis  right now. There was a similar crisis 100 years
ago. David Hilbert, who was one of the leading  mathematicians in the early 20th century,
had this great dream finding that every  single open problem in mathematics should
be solved or unsolved. We should systematically  try to answer all the questions in our subject.
Here’s a famous quote in German: “Wir müssen  wissen, und wir werden wissen,” “we must know,
and we will know.” Now, this was the  rallying cry for mathematics in 1900.
Gödel proved this very, very striking result  that no matter how you set out the rules of
mathematics, there will always be statements  that cannot be proven or disproven from those
rules alone. That there is no fixed set of laws  of logic that can answer every single question.
They will always be incomplete. This was very  traumatic for mathematicians. It said that
Hilbert’s program would never be finished in some  sense. Over time, I think, we acclimatized to it.
In practice, many of the results that we  do care about, we can prove or disprove.
The specific statements that Gödel showed  which were not provable or decidable are
not the ones that we encounter in real  life. Sometimes there are questions that
you can’t answer using the usual axioms or  rules that you’re allowed to use normally,
but sometimes we add new rules. There are other  foundations of mathematics which can prove more
things than the standard ones. Sometimes we do  play with different rules, like when you play
chess. There are some standard rules of chess,  but sometimes we also consider other variants.
We’ve moved to a more pluralistic view  of mathematics, where there isn’t just
one true mathematics and one universal true  and false facts. There is a standard one,
but we do also consider more exotic alternate  types of mathematics, where we have more rules
or fewer rules, and there’s a multiverse of  different types of mathematics to play with.
We have different number systems.  We have different geometries.
Mathematics has evolved over time to just a more  pluralistic view of everything. We are comfortable
with it now, but it was a very uneasy feeling to  discover this result in 1930, that your worldview
of mathematics changed. It’s as if you thought the  Earth was stationary, and now you know it moves.
COWEN: Is it fair to say your overall  approach to the foundations of math is
quite pragmatic? It’s not Hilbert,  it’s not Brouwer. There’s really
no result that could come along that  would make you feel nihilistic. It’s
just there’s different avenues to explore  things. Is your view different than that?
TAO: Yes. I try to have some humility. There  are certain mathematical models that I like,
and I think they explain the real world.  There have been revolutions in the past
where quantum mechanics, you mentioned, was a  very big philosophical transition in physics.
We are currently going through a transition  where most of mathematics was human-generated,
and we’re now entering an era where  proofs are being generated by AI.
This is also changing our philosophical  foundations of what does it mean to prove
something. What does it mean to understand  something? As I said, these two statements
used to be almost synonymous, and now they have  been decoupled quite severely. I try to keep an
open mind, which I think is part of what it  means to be a good scientist. You don’t have
a dogmatic view of what science is or isn’t.  You update it based on events and new data.
COWEN: How much do you read in the earlier  history of mathematics, say, 19th century,
early 20th century? Do you learn by doing that,  or it’s just a fun thing you do as a hobby?
TAO: I think mathematics is about stories a  lot more than is normally presented. If you
take a math class, maybe you might hear some  stories about there was a mathematician called
Évariste Galois, who died in a duel. He was  writing very frantically the basis of what
we now call Galois theory the night before the  duel because he was certain he was going to die,
and he did. There are lots of wonderful  stories that make the subject come alive.
Unfortunately, often when you present them  in classes, you take out all the backstory
and the side context, often because of lack of  time. There’s a lot of math that you want to
give to your students. Math often comes across as  just a bunch of equations and rules and recipes.
I do find that reading the histories makes  it come alive. There are some really good
stories in the history of mathematics, which,  luckily, they make for great podcast stories
and YouTube videos. Maybe they do get heard  by the public, but not in classrooms so much.
COWEN: How much of abstract mathematics do  you feel is useful? Is it like a lottery
ticket where maybe one in every 200 things  is useful, but it’s clearly worth doing,
or is your view that if we knew everything,  explored all angles, it would all fit together,
and every part of it would be a unified  whole that could be used for something?
TAO: Right. I view STEM as a whole—science,  technology, engineering, and mathematics—as
an ecosystem, and mathematics is the soil. It’s at  the foundations. It doesn’t generate the fruits,
the things that are most directly useful for  humans, but it sets the stage. Of course,
it gives us all the formulas and recipes that  other scientists use. It also sets limits.
Most other sciences or engineering, they tell  you what’s possible. You can build a rocket,
and it flies, and now you’ve proven  that it is possible for a rocket to fly.
If you want to show that something’s impossible,  that there's a limit, for example, if you want to
communicate using a wireless spectrum, what is  the maximum amount of bits you can stream from
A to B? There’s a branch of mathematics,  information theory, that tells you this, and
it gives you limits. There’s a maximum theoretical  limit, and you can’t discover this by engineering.
You can send more and more bits down a channel,
but only mathematics can tell you that there’s  a limit. This is useful because it tells you
how close you are to perfection, and when  to stop trying to develop an even better
wireless encoding protocol because you’re  already at 98 percent of mathematical capacity.
There’s really no point to spend another  $1 million trying to make it any better.
Mathematics unifies science.  It gives a common language,
so scientists get to talk to other  scientists. Whether something’s useful
or not, it often takes decades. Shannon’s  information theory came out in the ’40s,
but it’s only when cellphones came along and  big data that it really became so essential
to the modern economy. Even if a topic is  useless now, who knows in 20 years, 40 years.
COWEN: When string theory is presented to you,  viewing it just as a mathematician, does it feel
beautiful to you, or do you think this is strange  and awkward, it’s not intuitive enough? What’s
this higher number of dimensions doing here?  Is it interesting math to you? What is it?
TAO: This is less of my field. The  ideas from string theory have impacted
geometry quite a lot. The modern field of  mathematical geometry already studies very
high-dimensional objects and making them even  higher dimensional by turning points into little
strings, they’re very comfortable with that.  My understanding is that the ideas proposed
by physicists have inspired mathematicians to  solve many geometry problems in their own field.
Now, my understanding also—I’m not really a  physicist, though—is that while the theory
is very beautiful, it could have been a good  explanation of the real world, but we have
not found a really striking confirmation that  string theory really is a good model. One of the
objections that I’ve heard is that it’s actually  too flexible a theory. There are too many ways
in which these strings can vibrate. While they  can explain our current universe, they can also
explain trillions and trillions of other alternate  universes, and there’s no obvious way to explain
why we live in this one and not in all the other  universes that are compatible with string theory.
I don’t know to what extent string theory  is still the leading proposal for, say,
quantum gravity, which is one of the  big goals of modern theoretical physics,
to unify quantum mechanics and gravity.  There was a lot of hope that string theory
would do this. They’ve tried for many decades.  I think that there’s still no really conclusive
evidence that it’s working. I think people  are beginning to explore other alternatives
to string theory as well, but you may have to  talk to a physicist for the latest on that.
COWEN: Reading your book, I  come away with the gut feeling,
a purely subjective impression, but that  you love geometry most. Is that justified?
TAO: I love all kinds of mathematics. Maybe I like
it because I’m not as good at it  as with other types of mathematics.
There are mathematicians who are very visual, and  they can see a complicated shape and rotate it in
their mind. I can’t do that. I actually have to  write things out and use visual aids, blackboards,
to really see geometry. I have to put some  real effort to understand geometric ideas.
Maybe because of that effort, the ones that I  do understand, I actually find quite beautiful.
My native field is actually more analysis.  I like understanding what things are big,
what things are small. If you add a  whole bunch of small things together,
can you get something big? When  do waves interfere constructively,
destructively? That type of mathematics feels very  natural to me. I try to appreciate all kinds of
mathematics. I’ve learned a lot by talking to  fellow colleagues who think about mathematics
in a different way. I’ve learned a lot from them,  and hopefully, they’ve learned something from me.
COWEN: With respect to real analysis,  why does that come so relatively late
in the history of math? It doesn’t seem that  difficult in a way, once it occurs to you,
that there’s such a thing at all, even  if some of the results are difficult.
TAO: Traditionally, mathematics was about  exact formulas and numbers: 2 + 3 is exactly 5.
It’s only when we started dealing with really  large quantities, like astronomical scales of
numbers or big data, whatever, that we  needed to start working approximately.
If you want to know the GDP of the United  States, you don’t need it for the nearest penny.
Just getting the first few digits is enough.  It took a while to figure out what was the
mathematics for orders of magnitude, and  I talked about what happens in the limit.
If instead of working in a family of  five people or a village of 100 people,
you work with hundreds of millions of people,  you actually really want to send the number
of people off to infinity and ask, what is going  on in the infinite limit? Often, the mathematics
becomes simpler. It’s like if you want to  model a whole bunch of particles of a fluid,
you could model all the trillions of particles  bouncing around, but actually, it’s easier to
think of it as a continuous object and talk about  pressure and volume and macroscopic quantities.
Early mathematicians struggled a  lot with infinity. The Greeks had
all these paradoxes. They didn’t understand how  infinity worked. It was a very nontrivial task.
It took centuries to work out how to  deal with infinity safely. It’s like
radioactive material. Not all the laws of  algebra work with infinity. It really has
to be handled with care, but it is very  powerful once you know how to use it.
COWEN: Zero as a number, that seems to come,
in a way, late in mathematics. That’s  what, the 7th century AD in India?
TAO: Yes.
COWEN: Zero seems so simple to  us. Why does that take so long?
TAO: Because it’s invisible. I think it’s human  nature to only give names to things that you
see. You see a sheep, that’s a sheep. You see  two sheep, that’s two sheep. You see nothing,
you don’t say, “I see zero sheep.” It is a  conceptual leap. It requires some abstraction.
People inferred the need for zero by manipulating  the numbers that they could see. In fact, I think
there are many languages where they don’t even  have a name for one. The counting system starts
at two. Even the idea that a single object you  can attach a count, one, to it, that’s already a
conceptual leap. You may think that if you see  a sheep, you don’t need to call it one sheep.
People had to work with numbers of two, three,  four, five, and they started applying rules to
these numbers. They discovered addition and  subtraction and other arithmetic operations.
Just by following the rules of what  these operations were trying to do,
they were naturally led to consider new  numbers: one, zero, negative numbers, fractions,
square roots. These are numbers that are not  obvious. You can’t see −3 sheep or √2 sheep.
Once you trust in the laws of arithmetic, and you  just accept that they are predicting other numbers
to exist and be useful, then we found them. Now  we teach them in our primary school classes,
so it’s obvious to us. We’ve internalized  things like zero. It was a major conceptual
breakthrough back in the 7th century,  as you say. We shouldn’t mock these
ancient mathematicians for  not knowing what zero was.
COWEN: When you look at mathematical economics  over the last two decades, is it interesting to
you as math, or is it just a bunch of people doing  something different that, to you, is low level?
TAO: Oh, yes, I was always fascinated by  economics. I love game theory, and actually often
there are pure math problems where it’s actually  good to think in game theory terms. In analysis,
you have all these complicated statements, like  for every ε, there exists a δ, blah, blah, blah.
It looks very intimidating, but if you phrase it  as a game, your opponent is giving you an ε, you
need to counter that ε with a δ of your own. If  you view it as a game, then actually you can talk
about strategies and who’s ahead, who’s behind. It  actually activates really good modes of thinking.
I’ve used economic thinking in my own  work. We talk about cost functions and
minimizing loss. There are lots of concepts.  Ricardo’s law of comparative advantage,
I use that to run my life. There are so  many things I can do. What do I choose
to spend my time on? It’s actually a very  useful principle: comparative advantage.
Economics, I find it’s a very good arena to  understand the difference between models and
reality. Physics, we’re spoiled because  we’ve had these great physicists who’ve
created these very accurate models of the real  world, classical mechanics, quantum mechanics,
and they’re very well tested and very  accurate. You can just go to town exploring
their consequences and still predict reality.  Economics is a much more mixed situation where
you have models, and sometimes they predict the  real world very well, but sometimes they don’t.
In addition to doing the math, you also have  to do the modeling, and you have to understand
the limits of when a model starts breaking  down and what you need to do to adjust it.
I find that fascinating. It’s somewhere between  the hard sciences and the social sciences. There’s
enough hard models that you can do math, but  there’s also enough real-world messiness that you
have to also grapple with the subjectivity. As an  outsider, I find it a really fascinating subject.
COWEN: When you looked at the Black-Scholes model,
were you shocked when the probability  doesn’t matter? Was that beautiful to you?
TAO: Yes, yes, yes. There is a special feature of  Gaussian fluctuations that you can price options
just by knowing risk. There is one algebraic  miracle that makes this work. Normally,
predicting future costs of anything  is just an intractable problem,
and there just happens to be this miracle.  If you have Gaussian fluctuations,
then it is beautiful. This is actually a  really good example of when you need to
know when the models work and when they don’t  work. If you don’t have Gaussian fluctuations,
then actually Black-Scholes is somewhat dangerous  to use, especially if you compound it into
derivatives over and over again. Again, that’s  an old story. You know what happened in 2009.
COWEN: Nick Bostrom has a famous argument using  Bayesian analysis that probably we’re living in
a simulation. I’m not sure if he believes it, but  he doesn’t reject it. When you hear that argument,
are you, A, convinced, or B, you think  it’s somehow a misuse of mathematics?
TAO: I think it’s a good attempt. Bayesian  reasoning is very subtle because, as I said,
it’s already hard enough dealing with a  model because you don’t know whether the
model is accurate or not accurate. Bayesian  reasoning, you’re not just dealing with one
model of the world, but you’re dealing  with multiple models of the world,
and you have some prior belief as to how likely  each model is, and then you’re updating them.
It could be that you may be considering  two models, let’s say a hypothesis and
a null hypothesis, but there could be a third  hypothesis that you’re not considering at all,
which is actually the true explanation. If you  focus only on the two hypotheses that you can
think of, maybe it’s your lack of imagination,  which is actually blocking you from seeing the
real truth. You have to be aware of your own  limitations when you do Bayesian reasoning.
That said, you can use some reasoning like this.  There are certain models for the universe that
you can refute by pure reasoning. In ancient  times, people believed in prophecy and fate,
that certain people were destined to  have something happen 20 years from now,
but this is very incompatible with free will and  having laws of nature that are very predictable.
It’s also incompatible, to some extent, to being  in a simulation, for instance. You can do these
thought experiments, and you can play off various  grand philosophical ideas against each other.
You can play off the idea of simulation  against the idea of there being a creator.
One amusing thing I saw on  the internet recently is that
the fact that we can now create AIs that  appear smarter than us has theological
implications as to how intelligent  our creator was compared to ourselves.
COWEN: Yes.
TAO: It is entertaining to explore these  thought experiments, but you do have to be
very humble that we could be limited by our  own imagination. We are comparing different
models to explain the universe, but there  are infinitely many other models that could
also explain things and sometimes  we are just completely off track.
COWEN: Newcomb’s paradox. Are you a one-boxer or  a two-boxer? You sound like a one-boxer so far.
TAO: Oh, okay. I have to be reminded—
COWEN: That’s the Nozick problem from  the—well, it comes from Newcomb, of course,
but you can grab one box or two box, and  you’re told by a potentially omniscient
being that if you grab both boxes, you’ll end  up with less. The dominance principle tells
you to take both boxes. Expected utility  maximization says only take the one box.
TAO: Right. One thing that this paradox shows  you is that sometimes having more free will and
agency actually hurts you. You may think that the  more optionality and ability to think you have,
the better you’ll be off in life. That seems  intuitive. As I recall of Newcomb’s paradox,
if you lobotomize yourself to say, “I will  actually do surgery on my brain so that I cannot
take two boxes, I will only be able to take  one box,” then this being that is observing
you will see that, and it will reward  you. Whereas if you’re overthinking it,
then you may actually get penalized.
Newcomb’s paradox is actually an environment  where you are penalized for thinking too
much. It’s an exception to the rule that  being more rational is an advantage. It
is a nice thought experiment, but it may  have real-world implications. There are
actually some scenarios where you don’t  want to signal that you’re too smart.
COWEN: David Lewis has this famous article,  I think it’s 1982, where he argues the
repeated prisoner’s dilemma is a lot like  Newcomb’s paradox. This is a contested claim.
TAO: I can see that, yes. Actually, I saw a great  talk about this recently, that if you automate
your prisoner’s dilemma strategy with a computer  program and everyone gets to see your computer
program—it’s a very simple strategy, like maybe  you cooperate unless you saw someone defect, and
then you defect yourself. If you signal in advance  what you do and you remove your own free will,
then you can actually do better in the game  because people will see that you’re trusted.
There was this debate about a year ago: If you’re  a woman, would you rather be with a man or a bear?
Many women said they feel safer with a bear,  and I think one of the reasons is that the bear
has a much higher rationality. It’s much more  predictable what the bear will do, and the fact
that interacting with someone who is really  intelligent actually adds risk. There’s lots
of games like that. I think the game of chicken  is another game where one of the strategies to
win chicken is to actually disable your steering  wheel and just go full speed ahead, but visibly
throw away your steering wheel. Then the rational  strategy for the other player is to swerve.
