COWEN: Let’s say we put you in charge  of math education in the United States.
Put aside AI. We’ll get to that in a bit.  How would you improve math education here?
TAO: Oh, that is a really complex problem.  My main experience with education is at the
university level. I’m at a fairly prestigious  university where we are quite selective,
so we get among the best students coming  from both the American and overseas high
schools. I don’t have the best view of what’s  going on at the K-12 level. I talk to people,
and I have two kids who have gone through the K-12  system, but that’s really a small amount of data.
COWEN: Wasn’t there a recent report  that UCLA faculty complained that a
lot of the entering students didn’t even  have great middle school math? Some do,
some are excellent. I’ve taught in  the UC system, but it’s high variance.
TAO: Yes. There was a report from UC San  Diego in particular that was quite concerning
about the basic readiness of many of the  students. I’m not sure whether it’s because our
selection system needs fixing. There’s  a debate to reinstate the SAT in the UC.
Or whether it’s because of COVID. That could be  a consequence. Some people say that social media
has destroyed the attention spans of school  kids. We don’t know. There are people who try
to systematically study education quantitatively  and try to see what types of pedagogy work best,
but it is a very soft science. I think  some of the findings are controversial.
I do think we need lots of experiments, and  some way to scale up experiments that work
on a single school to the whole system. I do know  that there have been lots of little experiments.
Let’s flip the classes. Let’s ban technology, or  let’s do things in a different way. When you do
it on a small scale, it can be great. When you  have some teachers who are really enthusiastic
about this experiment and the kids are excited  about trying something new, you can get these
fantastic results. Then you try to deploy them  to 100 schools, and suddenly it doesn’t work.
One big issue is getting from a prototype  experiment to a large-scale deployment.
This I don’t know how to solve.  There’s some pragmatic realities of
just how education works at a typical,  let’s say, American high school, that
you can’t ignore just because something  works in some nice lab school experiment.
COWEN: Many of my economist friends, they think
we should teach less trigonometry  and more statistics. Do you agree?
TAO: Yes, I think that is a tweak. Traditionally,  the college math syllabus consists of a lot of
calculus, because for the classic applications  to physics and engineering and the hard sciences,
calculus was almost the most important  higher math skill that you needed.
In the era of big data, statistics  and now machine learning and linear
algebra and probability are becoming more  important. We are making some tweaks there.
Although mathematics is often not about  the specific tools that you learn,
but just how to deal with abstract  situations and how to problem-solve.
I view math as a good playground to think where  the cost of failure is cheap. In the real world,
if you do something in the real world and you make  a mistake, it could be very expensive. If you’re a
civil engineer and you’re tasked to build a bridge  and you make a mistake and the bridge collapses,
you made a very expensive mistake. If you’re  a surgeon and you cut the wrong thing,
you’ve made a very fatal mistake, perhaps. If you  have a math problem and you solve it incorrectly,
you just have wasted half an hour of your  time, but you can go back and do it again.
The specific tools you learn in math are somewhat  useful, but actually just the ability to play and
try to solve problems when there’s some unknowns  and things you don’t understand. How do you even
start? How do you set up the model? How do you not  get terrified of all the possibilities, and how to
not get paralyzed when you’re faced with anything  complex. That, I think, is the valuable skill, the
most valuable. All the other stuff you can look up  or even consult an AI now if you really wanted to.
COWEN: You did a math Olympiad  when you were 10. Should there
be some kind of embedded calculus option  in 7th grade that, if you want to do it,
you can just learn calculus early on, and if  kids don’t want to do it, they don’t have to?
TAO: There are Advanced Placement-type exams,  and there are math enrichment. There’s math
clubs. I think it’s good to have a lot of options  like this. They shouldn’t be mandatory. I think
if a kid doesn’t want to do these  things and you push them into this,
they will just have a horrible  time and end up hating mathematics.
Whether you want to formally include  this in the standard school system,
I think there could be special schools where they  have experts, and they really make an effort to
integrate these competitions and nonstandard  classes into their framework. It can work,
I think, when there is the supporting  infrastructure—so qualified teachers,
supportive administration, and just general  rules for how a student can choose these
activities in place of standard classes,  but it may not scale to the average school.
There may not be enough qualified teachers. Some  schools may have policies that are just somehow
not compatible. There may be too many parents  in one school that just do not like this type
of education. I think these options should exist,  and it should be possible for parents and kids
to select among several school options, some of  which would offer these and some of which don’t.
COWEN: How do you feel about quant finance?  Do you view it as a brain drain out of math,
or the potentially high wages overall attract  more talent into math, and some of the people
still end up doing things in mathematics, so the  net effect on math is positive? What’s your view?
TAO: On the one hand, mathematics,  like academia in general, we don’t
have enough positions in academia. Academia is  a fairly small sector of the economy. We train
many more students than can end up having  academic jobs. As a very practical matter,
we need other industries that also value  mathematicians and can hire people with, say,
math PhDs. Quantitative finance has been very  good at that, so often they actually pay very,
very well, better than academics  in many cases. I think that’s fine.
There are many positive uses of quantitative  finance. Used properly, you can price things well,
you can get accurate market signals, you can  get liquidity. If you pursue the wrong metrics
too much, you can also destabilize economies  and create crashes. It impacts the real world,
so you have to be more aware of these issues  than if you were just a pure mathematician.
There have been mathematicians who were very  successful in finance and gave back to the
math community. Jim Simons is one example. He  founded Renaissance Technologies. He made many,
many billions of dollars, and actually, he  founded the Simons Foundation, which is now
a major sponsor of pure mathematics and physics  and astronomy and computer science. It works out.
I do think academics do need to get out of the  ivory tower sometimes and engage with various
industries—finance, the tech industry. Here  at UCLA, we’re close to Hollywood, we had a
lot of ties with computer graphics industries,  for instance, and the movie industry. There are
many sectors of the economy now which are  becoming more mathematized. They need people
with good math skills, and we should  engage with all of them, I think.
COWEN: How long do you think it will  be before AIs create the equivalent of
new Millennium Problems for mathematics? Is that  two years away, 20 years away? Interesting ones.
TAO: It’s extremely uncertain times  now. I think a lot of assumptions
about how mathematics operates is going  to change a lot. There’s so many changes,
but in one sentence, we have moved from an  era of proof scarcity to proof abundance.
It used to be that proofs were really hard  and valuable, and so we would create these
open problems as these goals, these  landmarks, and we would march toward
these goals very slowly and deliberately, but  we’d pick up all these insights and techniques
and learn all these things along the way.  We have these Millennium Prize Problems,
and we have these targets that guided us, but  they’re relatively few in number. There’s only
seven Millennium Prize Problems. That was the  way things worked in a proof-scarcity era.
I think going forward, the idea of  focusing on individual problems,
that currency has basically been hyperinflated.  We now have machines that can just brute-force,
basically solve massive numbers of the old  problems that we used to use as landmarks,
and we have to really switch to some sort  of math 2.0. I think instead of dealing with
individual problems, we may start creating  huge datasets of thousands or millions of
problems and try to sweep them out. With this  AI, I can handle 30 percent of these problems.
Using this idea that this human contributed,  I can solve this 10 percent, but not pick out
individual problems per se anymore as the  goals, but work at a much higher scale.
I think that it will take a lot of cultural  shift. We are not used to mass production of
mathematics. We are still, in many  ways, in a pre-industrial economy,
math academia. We are forced, almost  at gunpoint right now, to switch to
an industrial or post-industrial economy, and  this will take quite a bit of cultural change,
but I think that’s what’s going to happen.  Individual problems, even like Millennium-level,
may disappear, and we will just have lots  and lots of big datasets of problems.
COWEN: On net, you’re happy? Unhappy?
TAO: That’s not the right word. It’s very  complicated. I’m excited by the possibility
of completely new types of mathematics  that didn’t exist before, but I’m also
actually quite horrified by the disruption,  which I think was much more than necessary.
Of course, every revolution, like the Industrial  Revolution, of course, is a famous example,
it creates job displacement and so forth. I  think there was some medium between status quo
and transition to a new paradigm where you had  more of the benefits of transition and fewer of
the disruptions. If the Industrial Revolution  happened within one month, it would have been
much more traumatic, entire careers cut short  with no ability to transition halfway through.
COWEN: It would have been better overall,
right? Like our standard of living,  people might have had in the 1950s.
TAO: Yes, but a lot might have been destroyed  permanently. There are still pre-industrial ways
of handcrafting certain objects or doing things  in a very old-school way. There are communities
that keep these more artisanal types of craft  alive, and they have cultural value. There was
enough time in the revolution to preserve these  culturally significant artifacts. It is possible
that there could be some major disaster where  we lose our power grid or something, and some of
these antiquated skills actually become relevant  again. Actually, from a strategic point of view,
there’s actually some value in preserving  what you might think of as obsolete skills.
Sometimes the historical insights of how an  obsolete practice developed can inform the
development of a modern skill. We talked about  the importance of history and mathematics. It’s
true. History is important everywhere. If you rush  the transition too much and you just focus on just
getting your productivity up or hitting some other  benchmark, you may lose some of this less tangible
value that you may only see after the fact what  you’ve lost. It’s like everything. If you want
to do urban development, you need to tear  down old buildings to create new ones, but
some buildings have actual historical value,  and there is a way to develop sustainably.
COWEN: Will the individual paper  still be the research unit for
human mathematicians, or will that change also?
TAO: I believe that will change, especially  since now AIs can generate that unit at a press
of a button. First of all, that unit used  to be bundled with other valuable things.
Traditionally, when a mathematician created  a paper, they also created a skilled author
who could then give talks about that  paper. They could go to conferences,
they could interact with other humans,  they could train students. Through that,
they can discover new connections, new  collaborations, new questions to ask.
Now we have these AIs that generate the  paper, but without all that extra value.
They have unbundled the PDF, the actual  physical paper, from the penumbra of more social
or intangible values of that paper. Also,  when a human solves those and writes a paper,
it came from first understanding the  problem and getting some insights,
and that you can communicate. The AI often  does not communicate what it learned when it
solves the problem. It just gives you the  output, but the process is very opaque.
On the one hand, I think papers will evolve  to show much more of the process. We have
focused a bit too much in the past on just showing  the finished product, but we’ve seen it in other
disciplines. Movies are enriched when you see  behind-the-scenes documentaries and lots of
extra material. People enjoy that extra content,  and I think papers will move in that direction.
I also think that we will also work at much  larger scales than papers. We will see entire
databases which are like the equivalent  of thousands of papers networked together
in a single spreadsheet, which you can  query and you can update in real time,
and you can get all these visualizations, which  you just could not do with the old system. Or
every time you wanted a new way to visualize the  literature, someone has to write a new paper, and
you have to wait a year before you get a different  view. You should be able to see an entire field.
I think people will have to move to more  collaborative, big math projects. Instead of
a small number of people working on individual  papers and then contributing atomically to
the literature, the literature itself  would be a much more networked, living,
collaborative entity where both AIs and humans can  collaborate. I think this is the only way forward.
We’ve seen in recent months that brute  competition between humans and AIs is
becoming very counterproductive. People  are just racing to dump out a paper three
minutes before someone else with an AI is  generating almost exactly the same paper,
and everyone is cutting corners and making the  papers harder and harder to read just because
they want the priority. Priority used to be a  very good way to organize our field and encourage
people to produce results in a timely fashion.  The metric has become way too over-optimized now,
and we need to switch, as you say, to beyond  thinking at the scale of a single paper.
COWEN: Now, you had started a new “journal,” if  that’s the right word, where people submit video
talks rather than printed papers. Does that  now become more important or less important?
TAO: I believe exposition, in general,  has been undervalued in mathematics. We
used to let the papers speak for themselves.  Proofs were scarce, and there were few enough
difficult papers that it worked that, when  a new result came out that was interesting,
everyone dropped what they were doing and read  those papers. Now, the flood of papers coming out,
in every field, there are 10 times, 100 times  more interesting papers than people can read.
The bottleneck is now, what are the results  that can be explained human to human? Papers are
actually a very terrible way to communicate. Most  people have not had the experience of reading an
academic paper, but it’s much easier if you can  interact with a human expert and ask questions,
use body language, use some visual aids.  Talks have been one of the traditional ways
in which we do that. We view these as secondary  byproducts of research, but I think, increasingly,
they will become one of the primary outputs,  especially since papers can be generated now
by AIs. Having the human-to-human  experience is increasingly valuable.
COWEN: Just for our last segment,
a few questions about you. What is  your favorite Hong Kong action movie?
TAO: Ha. It’s this half action movie, half comedy.  My favorite is called Kung Fu Hustle by Stephen
Chow. It came out about 20 years ago, back in the  golden age of Hong Kong cinema. I’ve not really
followed the modern era, but it is hilarious. It’s  an over-the-top parody of Hong Kong action movies.

It works best in the original Cantonese, but it  holds up in English. I recommend it to everybody.
COWEN: I like Drunken Master II, with  Jackie Chan. Do you know that one?
TAO: Yes, I watched it when I was a kid.
COWEN: Sometimes it’s retitled as just  Drunken Master. You have to be careful
with the edition because the first  Drunken Master is not that good.
TAO: Yes. The conceit is that he’s  a martial artist who becomes better
the more drunk he is. There’s this very  weird style. This is very typical golden
age Hong Kong action cinema. You  start with some ridiculous conceit,
and you just run with it, and you just play  it straight. That’s also a very good one.
COWEN: What do you find most beautiful in music?
TAO: I used to enjoy classical music when I was a  kid, especially Bach, the very intricate patterns.
Nowadays, sometimes I like epic instrumental  music, like the Lord of the Rings soundtrack or
something. Sometimes it inspires me into a working  mood. Sometimes I just need some random pop music
that is very familiar as comfort, some Taylor  Swift thing or something, something mindless.
Actually, it’s funny. I have access now. I can  play any piece of music now just by searching
on the internet very quickly. I actually listen  to it a lot less than when I had to have CDs and
things. It’s interesting. The more abundant  something is, sometimes the less you use it.
COWEN: Now, as an undergraduate,
you went to Flinders University in  Adelaide. That’s correct, in Australia?
TAO: Yes.
COWEN: Do you feel you somehow would have  done worse had you gone to Cambridge or
Princeton? Is it part of your success  that you had this unusual beginning?
TAO: Yes. My parents worked very hard to design an  education track that suited me. I skipped a lot of
grades. In fact, in math and science, I skipped  five grades. Emotionally and in the humanities,
I was not at that level, so I would also take  classes in physical education and English in
my regular year. I had this very complicated  schedule where, when I was in primary school,
I would take some classes in high school. When  I was in high school, I’d take math classes
at university. I enrolled in university at the  age of 13, I think, but I still lived at home.
Flinders University was a small university, but  it was a short drive from where we lived. I knew
all the faculty, and we were in small classes.  There was a particular math professor where we met
every week just for an hour, just talking math,  very casually. I took my classes, and actually,
I even failed some. I wasn’t actually the best  student, to be honest, but it was at my level.
COWEN: This is in math you failed some?
TAO: Yes, yes. Actually, quantum mechanics is also  a class that I failed. The two classes I failed
were Introduction to Fortran. I liked programming  in BASIC. I didn’t want to switch to Fortran, so I
refused to learn Fortran, and I failed the class.  Then Introduction to Quantum Mechanics, where the
class was half solving differential equations, and  that was fine, I liked doing the math, and half

I think actually not being in a super  competitive environment at the time,
but in a small place where everyone knew everyone  else, I felt on par with my other students, that
worked well for me. Then I went to Princeton as a  graduate student, and that was a much more elite
institution. I was shocked at how much my fellow  grad students knew a lot more math than I did.
It was in grad school that I failed the first  exam that I really did not expect to fail.
I failed two exams when I was an undergraduate,  but these were classes I didn’t care about,
and I expected to do badly. My qualifying exam  was an oral exam, and I actually learned I was

and he was very disappointed with me.  It actually changed my life. I actually
started studying it much harder and actually  putting real effort into explaining what I do.

COWEN: That’s quite an unusual  history. Today or more recently,

TAO: I am learning the power of  delegation more and more now. I
used to want to do everything myself, but I  am finding that my research collaborations,
trusting the junior people to take the  lead, working with students. Nowadays,
with the internet and AI, AI in particular,  it can be a very dehumanizing technology,

I’m finding that people rise to the challenge,  that if you give someone an ambitious task,

TAO: Yes. I’m 51 now, and yes, I am exhausted  quite a lot. This is another reason why I’m

COWEN: Very last topic, a very simple one.  Collatz conjecture: Is it true or false?
TAO: It’s true, but we have no idea how  to prove it, even with our fancy AIs.
The Collatz conjecture is sometimes called  the hailstone conjecture. You take a number.
If it’s odd, you make it bigger, you  multiply by 3 and add 1. If it’s even,
you make it smaller, you divide by 2. Then  you just iterate this over and over again,
and the numbers go bouncing up and  down like a hailstone. With hail,
every hailstone eventually lands and goes down to  Earth, and we think the same is true with Collatz,
that every number, it goes up and down, but it  will eventually hit 1, no matter what you do.
The first trillion numbers we’ve  tested do this. We also now know that,
in some sense, almost all numbers either  do this or come very close to this. We’ve
made some statistical progress on this conjecture,
but there’s always a chance that there’s this  one very special hailstone that just somehow,
instead of falling to Earth, just keeps floating  up and up, higher and higher, or maybe in a loop.
There could be one special exception or a  small number of exceptions, and we can’t
rule this out. It’s like if you’re at  a casino and you keep playing roulette,
most of the time you will lose because  the odds are in the casino’s favor. There
could be one special scenario where you  just keep winning over and over again,
and you just get richer and richer. Of course,  at some point, the casino will kick you out.
For Collatz, we can’t rule out that one  exceptionally lucky hailstone. None of
the ideas we have in mathematics come close to  ruling out this very extra special conspiracy.
I would love to know how to do that, but I don’t  think I’ll see that in my lifetime, even with AI.
